tweets.text: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use. 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will benevolently provide for humanity if sufficiently enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior. — http://shitter.thepixora.com/GavinSBaker/status/2088611616577253502#m

2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

In addition to transparency, I now believe frontier models should face mandatory third-party testing for cyber, bio, and autonomy risks—with the power to block or revoke deployment of models that pose catastrophic risk.

At Box, we've been testing Opus 5.5 on a variety of complex enterprise knowledge work tasks dealing with unstructured data with the Box Agent. Overall, we saw frontier capability levels, with major performance improvements over Opus 5. 63% fewer tokens used, 42% less verbosity, and 30% faster vs. Opus 5. And the model itself is cheaper, so this is a major win for any agentic computer use, coding, analytics, or data work that enterprises will be doing. Here are some examples of the task wins and performance gains across a variety of industry tests that we performed: • Financial services - due diligence (+39% task accuracy): A year of transaction records, with the job of finding every miscalculation in an acquisition target's pricing tool. Opus 5.5 scored a perfect result on every attempt in half the words Opus 5 used, consuming 82% fewer tokens overall. • Technology - cloud cost analysis (+65% task accuracy): Work out what a company should actually change about its cloud spend. Opus 5.5 picked the right basis for the retention calculation and kept the source data's unit conventions straight all the way through, so the number at the end actually holds up. It took half the time Opus 5 took, with 70% fewer tokens. • Consumer products - client account analysis (+17% task accuracy): Set the onboarding targets for a client account, reading across the signed contract, a satisfaction tracker and a team metrics sheet. The contract never states a senior/junior split, so Opus 5.5 derived it from the 18-person roster and showed the rule it used; several clients had a perfect 10 on individual survey questions, so it averaged each client's responses instead of crowning the single 10. It finished this one in half the time, on 78% fewer tokens. • Clinical diagnostics - data analysis (+15% task accuracy): Malaria rapid-test performance across a dry and a wet season: build the patient records out of two clinical PDFs, compute positive test rates by season and gender, and test whether parasite counts really differ between test-positive and test-negative patients. Opus 5.5 caught that the two groups' standard deviations differed more than 100-fold, re-ran it the right way, and found the dry-season difference didn't hold up after all. This accuracy gain came with a final answer that was half the length of Opus 5's, and also needed 78% fewer tokens end to end. highlights.text_fr: Aujourd'hui, nous avons annoncé la découverte, menée par Claude, d'une machine moléculaire qui pourrait représenter un nouveau mécanisme d'édition génétique. Sa fonction précise, son utilité biotechnologique (si tant est qu'il y en ait une), ou son niveau d'importance ne sont pas encore clairs, mais c'est un travail dont j'aurais été fier en tant qu'étudiant en doctorat. Le travail a été réalisé principalement, mais pas entièrement, par Claude : notre équipe des sciences de la vie a suggéré un vaste domaine de recherche, Claude a parcouru la littérature et de nombreuses données génomiques pour découvrir quelque chose d'intéressant, puis Claude a proposé des expériences pour vérifier la découverte et notre équipe les a menées à bien. Il est facile de rejeter cela comme un cas isolé ou une curiosité, mais nous avons observé à plusieurs reprises un schéma où la performance de l'IA dans de nouveaux domaines intellectuels passe de faible à surhumaine en quelques années. En 2023, les modèles avaient du mal à faire des maths au niveau d'un lycéen moyen. En 2024, ils ont commencé à bien réussir les compétitions de maths pour les meilleurs lycéens du pays, en 2025 ils ont commencé à résoudre des problèmes ouverts mineurs, début 2026 des problèmes ouverts plus significatifs, et fin 2026 ils commencent à résoudre les quelques problèmes ouverts majeurs en mathématiques. Nous pensons que l'IA pour la biologie suit une tendance exponentielle similaire. La principale différence entre la biologie et les mathématiques, bien sûr, est que les maths peuvent être faites purement théoriquement, tandis que la biologie nécessite des expérimentations. Certains ont utilisé cela pour en conclure que l'utilité de l'IA en biologie sera limitée. Nous pensons que c'est faux. Comme nous l'avons démontré aujourd'hui, les humains peuvent collaborer avec l'IA pour effectuer les expériences, valider des résultats clés en quelques semaines et, si nécessaire, travailler avec l'IA pour itérer sur leurs découvertes. À terme, il pourrait même être possible pour Claude lui-même de réaliser les expériences en toute sécurité en contrôlant de manière autonome l'équipement de laboratoire, avec des mesures de protection appropriées, mais nous ne le faisons pas aujourd'hui (notre laboratoire est également une installation BSL1/BSL2 qui ne manipule pas de matériaux dangereux pour l'homme). Plus largement, l'avancement biomédical comporte de nombreuses étapes — des découvertes fondamentales en biologie à la recherche translationnelle, la découverte de médicaments, les essais cliniques, et enfin la fourniture effective de médicaments et de soins de santé aux patients. Nous nous intéressons également à ces étapes ultérieures, mais le simple fait d'accélérer la première étape des découvertes biologiques fondamentales a le potentiel d'accélérer et d'élargir l'ensemble du processus. Améliorer notre compréhension de la biologie et affûter les outils des biologistes peut faire avancer toutes les étapes ultérieures, par exemple en identifiant de nouvelles cibles médicamenteuses, en trouvant de nouvelles modalités thérapeutiques, en permettant des mesures plus précises et en accélérant la boucle expérimentale qui elle-même accélère davantage notre compréhension de la biologie. Cela n'accélérera pas en soi les délais des essais cliniques, mais si cela réussit, cela pourrait augmenter considérablement le nombre de candidats prometteurs qui entrent dans le processus — une augmentation du débit même si la latence demeure. Dans Machines of Loving Grace, j'ai écrit sur le potentiel de l'IA à « guérir la plupart des maladies en 5 à 10 ans » — un objectif qui semble impossible, mais que je crois à peine possible si l'IA est appliquée à chaque étape du processus. La première étape est de montrer que l'IA peut d'abord aider, puis mener, des découvertes biologiques. La découverte de Claude est la dernière d'une série de travaux antérieurs connexes qui remontent à des décennies, commençant par des systèmes comme CRISPR, et se poursuivant avec des découvertes comme la recombinase pont et VIPR ces dernières années. Récemment, l'intérêt s'est accru pour les systèmes basés sur les enzymes de la transcriptase inverse (RT), l'enzyme sous-jacente au système identifié par Claude. Et plus récemment, une équipe de Stanford travaillant indépendamment a décrit un nouveau système RT avec un ensemble non codant associé qui est à certains égards similaire à celui trouvé par Claude, bien qu'il s'agisse de systèmes distincts qui ont évolué indépendamment l'un de l'autre. Je crois que nous ne sommes qu'au tout début de la découverte de tels systèmes et de leur développement en outils puissants pour la biotechnologie. Je suis fier des ressources qu'Anthropic a investies pour accélérer les bénéfices publics de l'IA à travers les sciences de la vie, et nous visons à la fois à faire croître notre équipe des sciences de la vie et à travailler avec d'autres scientifiques pour étendre cette approche à un large éventail de problèmes. Nous ne comprenons pas encore ce que fait ce système, mais seule une poignée de systèmes connus partagent ses caractéristiques, et tous sont capables de couper, copier et coller l'ADN. Historiquement, la découverte de tels systèmes programmables a contribué à révolutionner la médecine. CRISPR, par exemple, est maintenant la base des médicaments génétiques. Mais il faudra beaucoup plus de travail pour savoir ce que fait ce système et s'il peut être utilisé de la même manière.
highlights.text_original: Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism. Its precise function, biotechnological utility (if any), or level of significance is not yet clear, but at minimum it is work I would have been proud to do as a PhD student. The work was done mostly, though not entirely, by Claude: our life sciences team suggested a broad area of research, Claude read through the literature and a bunch of genome data and discovered something interesting, then Claude proposed experiments to verify the discovery and our team carried them out. It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. I believe that we’re at the very beginning of finding such systems and developing them into powerful tools for biotechnology. I’m proud of the resources Anthropic has invested in accelerating the public benefits of AI through the life sciences, and we’re aiming both to grow our life sciences team and to work with other scientists to extend this approach to a broad range of problems. If you have a proposal for a research collaboration or are interested in joining our life sciences team, please reach out. Anthropic (@AnthropicAI) Claude has discovered a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages. Beside the enzyme’s gene sits a long array of repeating DNA—a structure that looks somewhat similar to CRISPR. We don’t yet understand what this system does, but only a handful of known systems share its features, and all of them are able to cut, copy, and paste DNA. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. But it will take much more work to learn what this system does, and whether it can be put to similar use.

It’s easy to dismiss this as a one-off or curiosity, but we’ve repeatedly seen a pattern where AI performance in new intellectual domains goes from weak to superhuman in a matter of a few years. In 2023 models struggled to do math at the level of an average high-school student. In 2024 they started to do well on math competitions for the best high-schoolers in the country, in 2025 they started to solve minor open problems, in early 2026 more significant open problems, and in late 2026 they are beginning to solve the top few open problems in all of mathematics. We believe AI for biology is on a similar exponential trend. The main difference between biology and mathematics, of course, is that math can be done purely theoretically, while biology requires experimentation. Some have used this to draw the conclusion that AI’s utility in biology will be limited. We think this is wrong. As we’ve demonstrated today, humans can collaborate with AI to perform the experiments, validate key results in a few weeks and, if necessary, work with the AI to iterate on what they find. Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today (our lab is also a BSL1/BSL2 facility that doesn't handle materials dangerous to humans). More broadly, biomedical advancement has many stages — from fundamental biology discoveries, to translational research, to drug discovery, clinical trials, and finally the actual delivery of medicines and health care to patients. We are also interested in these later stages, but even simply accelerating the first stage of fundamental biological discoveries has the potential to speed up and broaden the entire pipeline. Improving our understanding of biology and sharpening biologists’ tools can drive forward all of the later stages, for example by identifying new drug targets, finding new therapeutic modalities, allowing for more precise measurement, and speeding up the experimental loop which itself further accelerates our understanding of biology. This will not in itself speed up clinical trial times, but if it succeeds it could greatly increase the number of promising candidates that go into the pipeline — an increase in throughput even though latency remains. In Machines of Loving Grace, I wrote about AI’s potential to “cure most diseases in 5-10 years” — a goal that sounds impossible, but one I believe is just barely possible if AI is applied to every stage of the pipeline. The first step is showing that AI can first help with, and then drive, biological discoveries. Claude’s discovery is the latest in a line of related prior work that goes back decades, beginning with systems like CRISPR, and continuing with discoveries like the bridge recombinase and VIPR in the past few years. Recently, there has been heightened interest in systems based on reverse transcriptase (RT) enzymes, the enzyme underlying the system Claude identified. And most recently, a Stanford team working independently described a novel RT system with an associated non-coding array that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found, though they are distinct systems that evolved independently from each other. Historically, the discovery of such programmable systems has helped revolutionize medicine. CRISPR, for instance, is now the foundation of genetic medicines. idees.text_fr: 1/2 Merci Gavin pour un échange particulièrement réfléchi. Je ne passe généralement pas beaucoup de temps sur les réseaux sociaux, mais je voulais m'engager ici car cela met vraiment en évidence le cœur d'une conversation importante. Premièrement, sur la réglementation, je pense que « soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la réglementation, soit la distribuer largement » est un faux choix. Je sais qu'il y a une sorte de raccourci à la Silicon Valley où réglementation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir, mais j'ai toujours trouvé que c'était une image trop simplifiée du monde. Beaucoup de gens en dehors de cette bulle pensent à la réglementation comme quelque chose qui contraint le pouvoir des entreprises et bénéficie aux gens ordinaires. Je ne suis pas nécessairement d'accord avec cette perspective non plus, je pense plutôt que c'est compliqué et que cela dépend vraiment de ce que la « réglementation » contient. Mais en particulier, je pense que ceux qui adoptent le cadre « réglementation = capture réglementaire = concentration du pouvoir » sous-estiment souvent le pouvoir décentralisateur des processus institutionnels objectifs et équitables. Une analogie grossière est que le système judiciaire formel peut parfois sembler guindé et élitiste, mais il fait un bien meilleur travail pour défendre les droits des individus vulnérables que l'alternative, la justice populaire. Au mieux, les institutions peuvent conférer le pouvoir aux idées plutôt qu'aux personnes, et ainsi décentraliser ce pouvoir. C'est pourquoi Anthropic a toujours formulé ses propositions politiques très soigneusement. Nous nous efforçons de faire des propositions qui désavantagent (ralentissent) les entreprises d'IA de pointe tout en *avantageant* les petits concurrents. Le SB53 de Californie (que nous avons soutenu), et même le très décrié SB 1047 (sur lequel nous étions ambivalents), exemptent complètement toute entreprise en dessous d'un certain montant de revenus ou de coûts d'entraînement de modèles d'être couverte du tout (c'était 500 millions de dollars pour le SB 53, moins pour le 1047 mais nous nous y sommes opposés). Plus récemment, le processus de test que nous avons préconisé au CAISI et à la Maison Blanche implique des tests plus rigoureux pour les modèles de pointe que pour les modèles hors pointe — quelque chose qui avantage différemment les challengers. De même, la lettre « Pacing the Frontier » envisage (ou du moins l'implémentation préférée d'Anthropic l'envisage) de moduler le rythme des meilleurs modèles tout en ne contraignant pas ceux qui rattrapent leur retard. Cela nuit aux intérêts commerciaux des laboratoires de pointe et aide les challengers, y compris les modèles à poids ouverts ! Globalement, mon point de vue est que l'IA est *structurellement* une technologie qui tend à concentrer le pouvoir, pour des raisons qui n'ont rien à voir avec la réglementation (plutôt avec les implications extrêmes des lois de mise à l'échelle). Les poids ouverts aident un peu à cela, mais sont loin d'être une solution suffisante car ils ne font que déplacer la concentration vers ceux qui ont le plus de calcul et de puces (qui sont grosso modo les laboratoires de pointe plus peut-être les fournisseurs de matériel). En revanche, je pense que les bonnes « règles de conduite » peuvent simultanément (a) aborder les risques cyber/bio/d'alignement de l'IA, (b) contraindre institutionnellement le pouvoir des entreprises d'IA de pointe, et (c) laisser de la place aux modèles à poids ouverts tout en abordant les risques spécifiques qu'ils entraînent. D'ailleurs, je ne pense pas que les événements des derniers mois aient « échoué à aboutir à [mon] chemin réglementaire préféré ». L'approche que l'administration Trump serait en train d'adopter — des tests avant le déploiement pour les modèles de pointe, et aussi des tests des modèles à poids ouverts lorsqu'ils se rapprochent de la pointe — est une approche que je soutiens beaucoup, même si bien sûr je dois en voir les détails pour en être sûr. Je soutiens également les idées de Demis Hassabis concernant une entité de type FINRA. Cela contraste avec il y a six mois, lorsque la plupart de l'industrie poussait encore à la préemption de toute réglementation étatique et à aucune approche fédérale apparente. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, merci d'avoir remis les pendules à l'heure. Le problème plus large est que plusieurs personnes très sérieuses de la Silicon Valley ont entendu une variante de cela et la croient vraie. Et la raison pour laquelle c'est crédible pour tant de gens est que c'est cohérent avec le message public de Dario et ce qu'il a exposé dans l'essai que vous avez partagé : cette technologie *pourrait* être dangereuse pour les humains de multiples façons, pourrait conduire à une concentration extrême du pouvoir économique (comme exposé dans l'essai) et doit donc être réglementée de manière réfléchie. Je suis d'accord avec les risques potentiels et je crois que Dario formule tous ces arguments de bonne foi. Comme discuté dans le podcast, si l'on convient que l'IA *pourrait* être dangereuse, il existe deux façons d'aborder ce risque potentiel. Soit la concentrer entre les mains de quelques entreprises et politiciens choisis via la réglementation, soit la distribuer largement. Cela se résume essentiellement à savoir si l'on croit que l'IA est trop dangereuse à concentrer ou trop dangereuse à distribuer. Il y a des arguments raisonnables des deux côtés, mais je suis profondément d'accord avec la déclaration de Zuckerberg : « La notion que l'IA est si dangereuse que la seule voie sûre est une concentration extrême du pouvoir semble intrinsèquement problématique. Historiquement, espérer qu'un pouvoir absolu pourvoira bénévolement à l'humanité s'il est suffisamment éclairé n'a pas conduit à des résultats sûrs ou positifs. » Et comme le dit Dario dans l'essai susmentionné, « certains objecteront que nous pouvons simplement contrôler les IA avec un équilibre des pouvoirs entre de nombreux systèmes d'IA, comme nous le faisons avec les humains. » Je crois que c'est la meilleure voie à suivre : je veux autant d'IA que possible pour maximiser les chances qu'une d'elles partage mes propres valeurs. Et comme Dario le note, aucun humain n'a jamais été capable de prendre le monde. À ce stade, je pense qu'il est juste de dire que Dario a perdu l'argument. Son message n'a pas abouti à son chemin réglementaire préféré. Le fait que la seule solution à l'incident récent où un modèle OpenAI avancé non publié a piraté Hugging Face ait été un modèle open-source a probablement mis fin à toute chance de réglementation stricte à court terme. Essentiellement, toutes les grandes entreprises sauf Anthropic ont signé la lettre de Jensen. Cependant, le message de Dario a été massivement utile aux efforts visant à interdire les centres de données ici en Amérique. Je soupçonne que nous verrons des groupes de défense anti-centres de données diffuser des publicités utilisant des extraits de Dario avertissant à quel point l'IA pourrait être dangereuse pour les humains. Ses efforts de bonne foi en faveur de la réglementation augmentent maintenant les chances que l'IA ne soit pas bénéfique pour les Américains et les humains partout dans le monde. Je crois qu'il y a une chance raisonnable que l'IA puisse nous aider à guérir la plupart des formes de maladies afin que nous ayons une durée de vie prolongée et puissions profiter de ces longues vies dans un futur abondant de type Star Trek. C'est l'avenir que je veux et je pense que Dario diminue les chances de cet avenir à ce stade. Il est sur le point d'être le PDG de l'une des entreprises publiques les plus importantes du monde et, étant donné que l'effort pro-réglementaire a échoué (du moins pour l'instant), je pense respectueusement qu'il devrait s'efforcer d'être un défenseur plus positif de sa propre industrie. Et si j'ai tort et que nous devons réglementer cette technologie, il sera un défenseur plus efficace à l'avenir, ayant été ouvert d'esprit à l'alternative. Et pour plus de clarté et comme je l'ai souligné dans le podcast, je pense qu'Anthropic a de profonds avantages concurrentiels et est une entreprise incroyable. Ironiquement, le principal risque que je voyais pour Anthropic il y a quelques mois était la nationalisation à la suite de la propre rhétorique et du comportement de Dario.
idees.text_original: 1/2 Thanks Gavin for an especially thoughtful exchange. I don't usually spend much time on social media but I wanted to engage here because it really brings out the heart of an important conversation. First, on regulation, I think that “either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely” is a false choice. I know that there’s a sort of Silicon Valley shorthand where regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power, but I’ve always found this to be an overly simplified picture of the world. Many people outside this bubble think of regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. I don’t necessarily agree with that perspective either, rather I think it’s complicated and really depends on what the “regulation” consists of. But in particular I think that those in the “regulation = regulatory capture = concentration of power” frame often underrate the decentralizing power of objective and fair institutional processes. A crude analogy is that the formal court system can sometimes feel stuffy and elitist, but it does a much better job of defending the rights of vulnerable individuals than the alternative, mob justice. At their best, institutions can vest power in ideas rather than people, and thereby decentralize that power. This is why Anthropic has always made its policy proposals very carefully. We try very hard to make proposals that disadvantage (slow down) frontier AI companies while *advantaging* smaller competitors. California’s SB53 (which we supported), and even the much-maligned SB 1047 (which we were ambivalent on), completely exempt any company below a certain amount of revenue or model training costs from being covered at all (it was $500M for SB 53, lower for 1047 but we objected to that). More recently the testing process we’ve advocated for at CAISI and the White House involves more rigorous tests for frontier models than off-frontier models — something that differentially advantages challengers. Similarly, the “Pacing the Frontier” letter envisions (or at least Anthropic’s preferred implementation of it envisions) modulating the pace of the very best models while not constraining those who are catching up. This hurts the business interests of the frontier labs and helps challengers, including open-weights! Overall my view is that AI is *structurally* a technology that tends to concentrate power, for reasons that have nothing to do with regulation (more to do with the extreme implications of the scaling laws). Open-weights do help some with this but are nowhere near a sufficient solution because they simply shift the concentration somewhat to those with the most compute and chips (which are roughly the frontier labs plus maybe hardware providers). By contrast I think the right “rules of the road” can simultaneously (a) address AI’s cyber/bio/alignment risks, (b) institutionally constrain the power of the frontier AI companies, and (c) leave room for open-weights models while also addressing the specific risks that they bring. BTW I do not think that the events of the last few months have “failed to result in [my] preferred regulatory path”. The approach that the Trump administration is reported to be taking — pre-deployment testing for frontier models, and also testing of open-weights models when they get closer to the frontier — is one that I am very supportive of, though of course I have to see the details to be sure. I am also supportive of Demis Hassabis’ ideas around a FINRA-like entity. This contrasts with six months ago when most of the industry was still pushing for preemption of all state regulation and no apparent federal approach either. Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) Sholto, thank you for setting the record straight. Larger issue is that multiple very serious people in Silicon Valley have heard some variation of this and believe it to be true. And the reason it is believable to so many is that it is consistent with Dario’s public messaging and what he outlined in the essay you shared: this technology *might* be dangerous for humans in multiple ways, could lead to extreme concentration of economic power (as outlined in the essay) and therefore needs to be regulated thoughtfully. I agree with the potential risks and I believe Dario makes all of these arguments in good faith. As discussed on the pod, if one agrees that AI *might* be dangerous, there are two ways to address this potential risk. Either concentrate it in the hands of a chosen few companies and politicians via regulation or distribute it widely. Essentially boils down to whether one believes AI is too dangerous to concentrate or too dangerous to distribute. There are reasonable arguments on both sides, but I profoundly agree with Zuckerberg’s statement that: “The notion that AI is so dangerous that the only safe path is an extreme concentration of power seems inherently problematic. Historically, hoping that an absolute power will bénévolently provide for humanity if suffisamment enlightened has not led to safe or positive outcomes.” And as Dario says in the aforementioned essay, “some may object that we can simply keep AIs in check with a balance of power between many AI systems, as we do with humans.” I believe this is the best path forward: I want as many AIs as possible to maximize the odds that one shares my own particular values. And as Dario notes, no human has ever been able to take over the world. At this point, I think safe to say that Dario has lost the argument. His messaging has failed to result in his preferred regulatory path. The fact that the only solution to the recent incident where an unreleased advanced OpenAI model hacked Hugging Face was an open-source model likely ended any chance of strict near-term regulation. Essentially every major company other than Anthropic has signed Jensen’s letter. However, Dario’s messaging has been massively helpful to efforts to ban datacenters here in America. I suspect we will see anti-datacenter advocacy groups runnings ads using clips of Dario warning about how dangerous AI could be for humans. His good faith efforts in favor of regulation are now increasing the odds that AI will not be beneficial for Americans and humans everywhere. I believe that there is a reasonable chance AI might help us cure most forms of disease such that we have extended lifespans and can enjoy these long lives in an abundant Star Trek like future. That is the future that I want and I think Dario is decreasing the odds of that future at this point. He is about to be the CEO of one of the most important public companies in the world and given that the pro-regulatory effort has failed (at least for now), I respectfully think he should make an effort to be a more positive advocate for his own industry. And if I am wrong and we do need to regulate this technology, he will be a more effective advocate for this in the future having been open-minded to the alternative. And for the sake of clarity and as I outlined on the pod, I think Anthropic has deep competitive advantages and is an amazing company. Ironically, the main risk I saw to Anthropic a few months ago was nationalization as a result of Dario’s own rhetoric and behavior.
idees.decryptage: Dario Amodei engage un débat sur la régulation de l'IA, s'opposant à l'idée simpliste que la régulation mène forcément à une "capture réglementaire" (où les règles sont dictées par les grandes entreprises). Il défend une régulation qui pourrait en fait décentraliser le pouvoir et aider les petits acteurs, notamment via des "modèles à poids ouverts" (dont le code est public). Les "lois de mise à l'échelle" sont des principes qui montrent comment la performance des IA s'améliore énormément avec plus de données et de puissance de calcul. Les "risques cyber/bio/d'alignement" désignent les dangers potentiels liés à la sécurité informatique, à la biologie (comme des agents pathogènes créés par IA) et au fait que l'IA n'agisse pas selon nos intentions. Une entité "FINRA-like" fait référence à un organisme indépendant d'autorégulation, comme la FINRA pour la finance aux États-Unis.

idees.text_fr: 2/2 Deuxièmement, concernant la communication autour de l'IA. Je ne suis pas d'accord pour dire que mon message a été disproportionnellement négatif. En fait, il a été à peu près également équilibré entre les risques et les avantages : j'ai écrit un essai majeur sur chacun, et même dans les interviews où je discute des risques, je m'assure de mentionner fréquemment les incroyables avantages ainsi que de proposer des solutions possibles aux risques (les courts extraits de mes interviews qui se retrouvent sur les réseaux sociaux ont tendance à être disproportionnellement négatifs, car cela génère des clics). En fait, j'ai écrit Machines of Loving Grace parce que je ne sentais pas que l'industrie de l'IA brossait un tableau suffisamment inspirant de la manière dont la technologie pourrait radicalement transformer le monde pour le mieux. La majeure partie de l'essai est consacrée à réfuter le scepticisme quant au potentiel de l'IA dans la santé et la biologie, et à montrer pourquoi je pense qu'il sera réellement possible de guérir la plupart des maladies humaines en environ 5 à 10 ans, aussi fou que cela puisse paraître aux gens ordinaires et franchement aux biologistes aussi (j'en étais un !). Et, si vous lisez mon essai le plus récent (Policy on the AI Exponential), je discute de propositions concrètes pour rationaliser le processus de la FDA afin de s'assurer que le déluge de médicaments accélérés par l'IA ne soit pas ralenti par le processus réglementaire. Je ressens l'urgence ici : j'ai perdu mon père à cause de l'Hépatite C quelques années seulement avant le développement d'antiviraux à action directe (sofosbuvir), qui guérissent 95% des patients et l'auraient probablement guéri. Je suis d'accord pour dire que le public a une vision négative de l'IA (et que c'est un gros problème), mais je ne pense pas que cela soit principalement causé par moi ou par tout autre leader de l'IA qui met en garde contre les risques de l'IA. Je pense que c'est fondamentalement une crise de confiance. Je pense que les gens ordinaires ne font pas confiance aux entreprises, aux gouvernements ou à l'industrie technologique et soupçonnent toujours que nous concoctons une nouvelle façon de les arnaquer. Les causes de cela remontent à des décennies et l'IA n'en est que la dernière itération. Je ne pense pas qu'une campagne marketing tape-à-l'œil avec une tournure positive (que certains ont préconisée pour Anthropic) soit la manière de regagner cette confiance — à ce stade, dire que l'IA va guérir le cancer est plus un cliché qu'une source d'inspiration, et la plupart des gens pensent que c'est trompeur. Ce qui fonctionnera, c'est de *réellement guérir le cancer*. Je pense que la critique la plus juste des entreprises d'IA, y compris Anthropic, est que nous n'avons pas encore tenu nos grandes promesses de bénéficier au monde. Cela nous incombe entièrement, et je pense que c'est la critique que vous devriez faire, au lieu de tout ce bla-bla sur la communication et le marketing. Nous faisons cependant de notre mieux pour y remédier : Anthropic intensifie très rapidement ses efforts en biologie et médecine, et nous espérons avoir des résultats incroyables dans les années à venir et quelques premiers aperçus dans les mois à venir. Lorsque nous aurons réellement accompli quelque chose de concret, le monde entier en entendra parler, aussi fort que possible, vous avez ma parole. Mais d'ici là, je ne veux pas faire de promesses en l'air, et en attendant, je me sens obligé de parler honnêtement des risques très réels de l'IA et de la manière de les aborder. L'honnêteté est la bonne chose sur le fond, et en termes de crédibilité publique et de confiance, ce n'est pas pire que, et peut en fait être meilleur que, une approche qui ignore ou détourne l'attention des risques que les gens perçoivent instinctivement comme réels.
idees.text_original: 2/2 Second, on the messaging around AI. I do not agree that my messaging has been disproportionately negative. In fact it has been about equally balanced between risks and benefits: I’ve written one major essay about each, and even in interviews where I discuss the risks, I make sure to frequently mention the incredible benefits as well as proposing possible solutions to the risks (short clips from my interviews that end up on social media tend to be disproportionately negative, as that gets clicks). In fact, I wrote Machines of Loving Grace because I didn’t feel the AI industry was painting an inspiring enough picture of how the technology could radically transform the world for the better. The bulk of the essay is devoted to refuting skepticism of AI’s potential in health and biology, and showing why I think it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in ~5-10 years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well (I used to be one!). And, if you read my most recent essay (Policy on the AI Exponential), I discuss concrete proposals for how to streamline the FDA process to make sure the deluge of AI-accelerated drugs isn’t slowed down by the regulatory process. I feel the urgency here: I lost my father to Hepatitis C only a few years before the development of direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir), which cure 95% of patients and probably would have cured him. I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks. I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing. We are however doing our best to fix this: Anthropic is ramping up its efforts very quickly in biology and medicine, and we hope to have incredible results in the coming years and some early glimmers in the coming months. When we’ve actually accomplished something real, the whole world will hear about it, as loudly as possible, you have my word on that. But until then I don’t want to make empty promises, and in the meantime I feel compelled to speak honestly about the very real risks of AI and how to address them. Honesty is the right thing on the merits, and in terms of public credibility and trust it is no worse than, and may in fact be better than, an approach that ignores or distracts from risks which people instinctively understand are real.

idees.text_fr: En plus de la transparence, je crois maintenant que les modèles de pointe devraient faire l'objet de tests obligatoires par des tiers pour les risques cyber, bio et d'autonomie — avec le pouvoir de bloquer ou de révoquer le déploiement des modèles qui posent un risque catastrophique.
idees.text_original: In addition to transparency, I now believe frontier models should face mandatory third-party testing for cyber, bio, and autonomy risks—with the power to block or revoke deployment of models that pose catastrophic risk.
idees.decryptage: Ce tweet, qui fait suite au débat sur la régulation, renforce la proposition de Dario Amodei concernant les risques liés à l'IA. Il suggère que les "modèles de frontière" (les IA les plus avancées) soient soumis à des tests indépendants pour évaluer les dangers liés à la cybersécurité (attaques informatiques), à la biologie (création de virus, par exemple) et à l'autonomie (l'IA prend des décisions imprévues), et qu'on puisse même interdire leur utilisation si les risques sont trop importants ('risques catastrophiques').

outils.text_fr: Google a lancé Gemini 3.8 Live, son nouveau modèle 'Speech to Speech', avec la variante 'Extended Thinking (High)' débutant à la 1ère place de l'indice 'Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech' à 82.6, et à la 1ère place de notre implémentation du benchmark 'Tau Voice' à 68.6%. Gemini 3.8 Live est le successeur de Gemini 3.1 Flash Live de @GoogleDeepMind, un modèle 'Speech to Speech' qui exécute des outils et des appels API en arrière-plan tout en poursuivant la conversation. Il existe en deux variantes : le Gemini 3.8 Live standard et le Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, qui prend en charge un effort de raisonnement configurable. Nous avons évalué le modèle standard et la variante Extended Thinking avec un effort de raisonnement élevé via l'API Gemini Live. Points clés : ➤ Indice 'Speech to Speech' : Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) débute à la 1ère place à 82.6, devant GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) à 81.5, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High à 81.3 et GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) à 80.1. Le Gemini 3.8 Live standard débute à la 5ème place à 76.0, les deux variantes étant en hausse par rapport à Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High à 71.5 (+11.1 et +4.5 points). L'indice moyenne le raisonnement vocal ('Big Bench Audio'), la performance agentique ('Tau Voice'), la préférence de l'arène et le taux de succès des tâches de l'arène. ➤ Arène d'agents vocaux : Gemini 3.8 Live se classe 2ème en préférence à Elo 1083, derrière Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (1096) et devant GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) à 1053, et 2ème en taux de succès des tâches à 93.2%, derrière Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High à 94.6%. Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) est en retrait à Elo 990 avec 89.1% de succès des tâches. ➤ 'Tau Voice' : Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) prend la première place de notre implémentation du benchmark Tau Voice à 68.6%, devant GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) à 67.9%, GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) à 59.3% et Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High à 56.5% - en hausse par rapport à 37.7% pour Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. Le Gemini 3.8 Live standard marque 30.1%. ➤ 'Big Bench Audio' : Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) marque 97.7% en raisonnement audio, devant Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High à 97.2% et derrière Qwen Audio 3.0 Realtime Plus à 99.2%. Le Gemini 3.8 Live standard marque 91.7%. ➤ Vitesse : Le temps moyen avant le premier audio sur Big Bench Audio est de 1.18 secondes pour Gemini 3.8 Live et de 1.35 secondes pour Extended Thinking (High), tous deux bien en avance sur Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High (2.99s) et en ligne avec GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) à 1.24s et GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) à 1.34s, bien que derrière Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High à 0.70s. ➤ Coût : Gemini 3.8 Live coûte 0.84$ par heure d'audio en entrée, le modèle le moins cher de l'indice et environ la moitié du coût de 1.75$ de Gemini 3.1 Flash Live High. Extended Thinking (High) coûte 3.50$ par heure - moins cher que GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) à 4.47$, Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High à 4.80$ et GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) à 5.83$, et environ 3.1x moins cher que GPT-Realtime-2.1 High à 10.75$.

The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference and Arena Task Success Rate ➤ Speech Agent Arena: Gemini 3.8 Live ranks #2 in preference at Elo 1083, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live (1096) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1053, and #2 on Task Success Rate at 93.2%, behind Grok Voice Think Fast 2.0 High at 94.6%. outils.decryptage: Ce tweet annonce le lancement de "Gemini 3.8 Live", un nouveau modèle d'IA "Speech to Speech" (qui peut traduire ou transformer la parole) de Google, avec des améliorations significatives. La variante "Extended Thinking (High)" signifie qu'il peut faire un effort de raisonnement plus poussé. Les termes comme "Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index" et "Tau Voice benchmark" sont des classements et des tests standards qui mesurent la performance des IA vocales en termes de compréhension, de capacité à utiliser des outils ("Agentic Performance"), de préférence des utilisateurs ("Arena Preference") et de succès des tâches ("Task Success Rate"). Les "appels API" sont des commandes utilisées par les développeurs pour faire interagir leur programme avec le modèle d'IA.
